\newcommand{\LoudOpening}{Part of speech prefers the head no more than a random lexical partition does}
\newcommand{\LoudVerdict}{The control is preferred more than part of speech in the all-model version only, so we claim no more than that part of speech is not preferred.}
\newcommand{\LoudNonSupSentence}{The one-sided test rejects any syntax-specific advantage as large as $+0.10$}
\newcommand{\QuietOpening}{Concepts prefer the tail no more than surface length does}
\newcommand{\QuietEquivalenceSentence}{This interval lies inside the pre-registered bound of $\pm0.10$ in both versions, so the quiet-tail specificity effect is not just undetected but smaller than the smallest effect we said would matter.}
\newcommand{\QuietAbstractEq}{and the effect lies inside a pre-registered equivalence bound of $\pm0.10$ retention units}
\newcommand{\HolmSentence}{After Holm correction, with all eight models, no member is significant; without gemma-2-2b, no member is significant.}
\newcommand{\KSweepSentence}{The mean $\Delta$ is significantly positive in 1 of 48 tail $\times$ layer $\times$ window $\times$ model-set cells, against about 1.2 expected by chance alone at two-sided $\alpha = 0.05$: loud mid at $k=0.5\%$ (all models only). It is significantly \emph{negative} (the control preferred over the real label) in 4 cells, at 3 settings: loud final at $k=5\%$ (all models only), loud final at $k=10\%$ (all models only) and loud mid at $k=10\%$ (with and without gemma-2-2b). No cell is interpreted on its own, because $k$ was fixed in advance; at the pre-registered $k$ the conclusion is as stated above, and no window size supports a specific effect.}
\newcommand{\LengthSentence}{Both stay inside the $\pm0.10$ equivalence bound, so the length control's correlation with the label does not drive the quiet-tail result.}
\newcommand{\MLPSentence}{so the conclusion is not specific to linear read-out.}
\newcommand{\ControlsOpening}{Part of speech also fails to beat type frequency and word length}
\newcommand{\PlacementSentence}{Placement and capacity are moderately related, in the expected direction: cells whose direction sits further in the tail tend to read the concept better from the tail. The relation is far from one-to-one: against the structural null the direction's energy sits in the tail in 30 of 60 cells, and in 15 of those is the concept also read better from the tail than from the head. And where capacity does favour the tail, it favours the length control just as much, so placement predicts where information is recoverable, not where the concept specifically lives.}
